claim: Spider venoms are a complex concoction of enzymes, polyamines, inorganic salts, and disulfide-rich peptides (DRPs).
source: Spider venoms are a complex concoction of enzymes, polyamines, inorganic salts, and disulfide-rich peptides (DRPs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 78 novel spider toxin superfamilies were identified in this study.
source: By evaluating DRPs under a comprehensive phylogenetic, structural and evolutionary framework, we have not only identified 78 novel spider toxin superfamilies but also provided the first evidence for their common origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The origin of spider toxin superfamilies is traced to 375 MYA in the common ancestor of Araneomorphae and Mygalomorphae.
source: We trace the origin of these toxin superfamilies to a primordial knot – which we name 'Adi Shakti', after the creator of the Universe according to Hindu mythology – 375 MYA in the common ancestor of Araneomorphae and Mygalomorphae.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on phylogenetic inference and evolutionary dating presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lineages under evaluation constitute nearly 60% of extant spiders.
source: As the lineages under evaluation constitute nearly 60% of extant spiders, our findings provide fascinating insights into the early evolution and diversification of the spider venom arsenal.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reference to taxonomic data.

claim: Reliance on a single molecular toxin scaffold by nearly all spiders is in complete contrast to most other venomous animals that have recruited diverse toxins with independent origins.
source: Reliance on a single molecular toxin scaffold by nearly all spiders is in complete contrast to most other venomous animals that have recruited into their venoms diverse toxins with independent origins.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analyses and comparison with other venomous animals.

claim: Venom deployment (e.g. prey capture or self-defense) influences evolutionary diversification of DRP toxin superfamilies.
source: Our results also suggest that venom deployment (e.g. prey capture or self-defense) influences evolutionary diversification of DRP toxin superfamilies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on molecular evolutionary analyses comparing offensive and defensive toxins.

claim: Spiders have mid-Cambrian or early Ordovician origin, nearly 495 million years ago (MYA; Lozano-Fernandez et al., 2016).
source: They are an archetypal arthropod group with mid-Cambrian or early Ordovician origin, nearly 495 million years ago (MYA; Lozano-Fernandez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lozano-Fernandez et al., 2016.

claim: Over 50,000 spider species and 129 families have been described to date (King, 2004; WSC, 2022).
source: They are amongst the most successful predators on the planet, with over 50,000 species and 129 families described to date (King, 2004; WSC, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to King, 2004 and WSC, 2022.

claim: The majority of spiders are equipped with chelicerae harbouring venom glands, with Symphytognathidae, Uloboridae, and certain Mesothelae species being the only exceptions (King, 2004; Mullen and Vetter, 2019).
source: The majority of spiders are equipped with chelicerae harbouring venom glands, with Symphytognathidae, Uloboridae, and certain Mesothelae species being the only exceptions (King, 2004; Mullen and Vetter, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to King, 2004 and Mullen and Vetter, 2019.

claim: Spider venoms are a concoction of enzymes, polyamines, nucleic acids, inorganic salts and disulfide-rich peptides (DRPs) (Senji Laxme et al., 2019b; King and Hardy, 2013).
source: Spider venoms are a concoction of enzymes, polyamines, nucleic acids, inorganic salts and disulfide-rich peptides (DRPs) (Senji Laxme et al., 2019b; King and Hardy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Senji Laxme et al., 2019b and King and Hardy, 2013.

claim: Spider venoms are predominantly rich in DRPs that are characterised by a diversity of structural motifs, including Kunitz (Yuan et al., 2008), disulfide-directed β-hairpin (Wang et al., 2000), disulfide-stabilised antiparallel β-hairpin stack (DABS; Pineda et al., 2020) and inhibitor cystine knot (ICK) – also known as knottins (Pallaghy et al., 1994; Undheim et al., 2016).
source: They are predominantly rich in DRPs that are characterised by a diversity of structural motifs, including Kunitz (Yuan et al., 2008), disulfide-directed β-hairpin (Wang et al., 2000), disulfide-stabilised antiparallel β-hairpin stack (DABS; Pineda et al., 2020) and inhibitor cystine knot (ICK) – also known as knottins (Pallaghy et al., 1994; Undheim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: DRPs constitute three-quarters of spider venom.
source: Despite the fact that DRPs constitute three-quarters of spider venom, our evolutionary understanding of their origin and diversification has remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The RTA clade from Araneomorphae constitutes over 58% of spider genera (2527 genera) described to date.
source: Here, we examined DRP sequences from the spiders of the Mygalomorphae infraorder (includes funnel-web spiders and tarantulas), family Theridiidae (includes the red-back spiders), and the Retrolateral Tibial Apophysis (RTA) clade from Araneomorphae, which constitutes over 58% of spider genera (2527 genera) described to date (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: 33 novel toxin superfamilies were identified from Mygalomorphae.
source: This approach enabled the identification of 33 novel toxin superfamilies along the breadth of Mygalomorphae (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence alignments and phylogenetic analyses shown in figures.

claim: Among the 33 novel Mygalomorphae toxin superfamilies, 31 belonged to the DRP class.
source: Among these, 31 superfamilies belonged to the DRP class, whereas the other two were enzymatic non-DRP toxins, including the first report of Neprilysin (SF103) and CAP (CRiSP/Allergen/PR-1; SF104) from Atracidae spiders (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis.

claim: Neprilysin (SF103) and CAP (SF104) are reported for the first time from Atracidae spiders.
source: Among these, 31 superfamilies belonged to the DRP class, whereas the other two were enzymatic non-DRP toxins, including the first report of Neprilysin (SF103) and CAP (CRiSP/Allergen/PR-1; SF104) from Atracidae spiders (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on sequence identification.

claim: 45 novel toxin superfamilies were identified from Araneomorphae.
source: Moreover, analyses of Araneomorphae toxin sequences using the strategy above resulted in the identification of 45 novel toxin superfamilies from Araneomorphae, all of which but one (SF109) belonged to the DRP class of toxins (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence alignments and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Among the 45 novel Araneomorphae toxin superfamilies, all but one (SF109) belonged to the DRP class.
source: Moreover, analyses of Araneomorphae toxin sequences using the strategy above resulted in the identification of 45 novel toxin superfamilies from Araneomorphae, all of which but one (SF109) belonged to the DRP class of toxins (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on sequence classification.

claim: Among all novel spider toxin superfamilies identified, the majority (n=75) were DRPs.
source: Overall, among all novel spider toxin superfamilies identified in this study, the majority (n=75) were DRPs, reinstating the dominance of this toxin type in spider venoms.
evidence: This is a summary finding based on the combined analysis of Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae toxins.

claim: DRPs can be segregated into ICK-like (n=28), DABS (n=13) and novel disulphide patterned non-ICK (n=34) superfamilies based on cysteine residue arrangement.
source: Based on the arrangement of cysteine residues involved in the formation of disulphide bonds, these DRPs could be further segregated into ICK-like (n=28), DABS (n=13) and novel disulphide patterned non-ICK (n=34) superfamilies (Pineda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a classification based on structural analysis of cysteine patterns.

claim: Novel toxin superfamilies were named after deities of death, destruction, and the underworld, following a nomenclature system introduced by Pineda et al., 2014.
source: We named these novel spider toxin superfamilies after deities of death, destruction, and the underworld (Supplementary file 1), following a nomenclature system introduced by Pineda et al., 2014.
evidence: This is stated explicitly and references the nomenclature convention.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses using Bayesian inference and maximum-likelihood approaches retrieved monophyletic groups of toxin superfamilies with high node support (ML:>90/100; BI:>0.95).
source: Reconstruction of evolutionary histories using Bayesian inference (BI) and maximum-likelihood (ML) approaches retrieved monophyletic groups of toxin superfamilies (Figures 2 and 3; node support: ML:>90/100; BI:>0.95; refer to figure supplement provided for complete phylogeny with branch lengths).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The plesiotypic DRP scaffold has undergone lineage-specific diversification in Mygalomorphae, leading to the origination of novel toxin superfamilies corresponding to each Linnaean genus.
source: Interestingly, the plesiotypic DRP scaffold seems to have undergone lineage-specific diversification in Mygalomorphae, where the selective diversification of the scaffold has led to the origination of novel toxin superfamilies corresponding to each Linnaean genus (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns observed in Figure 2.

claim: In Mygalomorphae, toxin scaffolds form distinct clades in phylogenetic tree reconstructions with high node support (ML:>90/100; BI:>0.95).
source: In our Bayesian and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree reconstructions, these toxin scaffolds were found to form distinct clades, further supporting this claim (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; node support: ML: ML:>90/100; BI:>0.95).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Araneomorph toxin superfamilies are scattered across spider lineages and form Linnaean family-specific groups.
source: As a result, and in contrast to mygalomorph DRPs, araneomorph toxin superfamilies were found to be scattered across spider lineages (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; node support: ML:>90/100; BI:>0.95).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Principal component analysis of toxin sequences provided evidence for the monophyly of mygalomorph and araneomorph superfamilies, where each toxin superfamily formed a distinct group.
source: Moreover, Principal component analysis (PCA) of toxin sequences further provided evidence for the monophyly of mygalomorph and araneomorph SFs, where each toxin superfamily formed a distinct group in PCA plots (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from PCA analyses shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Six cysteine residues were found to be nearly universally conserved across 101 DRP toxin superfamilies.
source: Six cysteine residues were found to be nearly universally conserved across 101 DRP toxin SFs (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence alignments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The origin of spider venom DRPs can be traced to Opisthothelae, the clade that encompasses Araneomorphae and Mygalomorphae (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
source: Our findings enabled us to trace the origin of spider venom DRPs in Opisthothelae, the clade that encompasses Araneomorphae and Mygalomorphae (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on phylogenetic analyses and supported by a citation.

claim: All DRP toxins in spiders may have had a common molecular origin, nearly 375 MYA.
source: Thus, we highlight for the first time that all DRP toxins in spiders may have had a common molecular origin, nearly 375 MYA.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on phylogenetic and evolutionary analyses.

claim: The majority of Mygalomorphae toxin superfamilies (12/19 SFs) have evolved under the influence of positive selection (ω ranging between 1.1 and 2.9; positively selected sites [PS]: 0–26).
source: Our findings suggest that the majority of Mygalomorphae toxin superfamilies (12/19 SFs) have evolved under the influence of positive selection (ω ranging between 1.1 and 2.9; positively selected sites [PS]: 0–26), while the remaining few have experienced negative or purifying selection (ω ranging between 0.7 and 0.8; PS: 0–13; Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular evolutionary analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: Nearly all Araneomorph toxin superfamilies investigated were found to have evolved under a strong influence of negative selection (ω ranging between 0.2 and 1.0; PS: 0–10).
source: In stark contrast, nearly all of the Araneomorph toxin superfamilies that we investigated here were found to have evolved under a strong influence of negative selection (ω ranging between 0.2 and 1.0; PS: 0–10; Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular evolutionary analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: Replacement changes in Mygalomorphae toxin superfamilies result in radical shifts in amino acid properties, potentially influencing their structure and function.
source: Outcomes of these analyses revealed the accumulation of replacement changes in Mygalomorphae toxin superfamilies that result in radical shifts in amino acid properties, potentially influencing their structure and function (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from TreeSAAP analyses assessing biochemical property changes.

claim: Toxin superfamilies SF74, SF77, SF79, SF89, SF90, SF92, and SF99 were identified as predatory toxins deployed for prey capture.
source: In these analyses, we identified toxin superfamilies SF74, SF77, SF79, SF89, SF90, SF92, and SF99 as predatory toxins (i.e. toxins deployed for prey capture – refer to the discussion section for the principle considered for this classification), whereas SF13 (i.e. Ares SF) was classified as a defensive spider venom toxin superfamily (i.e. toxins deployed for antipredator defence) as described previously (Herzig et al., 2020).
evidence: This classification is based on prior literature and the principle described in the discussion.

claim: SF13 (Ares SF) was classified as a defensive spider venom toxin superfamily deployed for antipredator defence as described previously (Herzig et al., 2020).
source: In these analyses, we identified toxin superfamilies SF74, SF77, SF79, SF89, SF90, SF92, and SF99 as predatory toxins (i.e. toxins deployed for prey capture – refer to the discussion section for the principle considered for this classification), whereas SF13 (i.e. Ares SF) was classified as a defensive spider venom toxin superfamily (i.e. toxins deployed for antipredator defence) as described previously (Herzig et al., 2020).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Herzig et al., 2020.

claim: Venom toxins employed for prey capture experience significant influence of positive selection (ω ranging between 1.2 and 2.9; PS: 0–11), relative to those used for antipredatory defence (ω=0.8; PS: 3).
source: Assessment of molecular evolutionary regimes identified a significant influence of positive selection on venom toxins that are employed for prey capture (ω ranging between 1.2 and 2.9; PS: 0–11, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), relative to those that are chiefly or exclusively used for antipredatory defence (ω=0.8; PS: 3; Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparative molecular evolutionary analyses.

claim: Prior attempts to explore the phylogenetic and evolutionary histories of spider venom DRPs have hypothesised independent origin and lineage-specific diversification of DRP venom toxins (Rodríguez de la Vega, 2005).
source: Prior attempts to explore the phylogenetic and evolutionary histories of spider venom DRPs have hypothesised independent origin and lineage-specific diversification of DRP venom toxins (Rodríguez de la Vega, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about prior literature supported by a citation.

claim: Recent literature suggests that the diverse disulfide-rich venom arsenal of Hadronyche infensa is a derivative of an ancestral ICK motif that underwent several rounds of duplication and diversification (Pineda et al., 2020).
source: In contrast, recent literature, primarily focusing on Hadronyche infensa, suggests that the diverse disulfide-rich venom arsenal of this Australian funnel-web spider is a derivative of an ancestral ICK motif that underwent several rounds of duplication and diversification (Pineda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about recent literature supported by a citation.

claim: 76 novel spider venom toxin superfamilies were identified (45 from Araneomorphae [44 DRP and 1 non-DRP] and 33 from Mygalomorphae spiders [31 DRP and 2 non-DRP]).
source: To address this knowledge gap, we employed sequence comparisons, phylogenetic inferences and evolutionary analyses, which enabled the identification of 76 novel spider venom toxin superfamilies (45 from Araneomorphae [44 DRP and 1 non-DRP] and 33 from Mygalomorphae spiders [31 DRP and 2 non-DRP]).
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the study.

claim: All extant spider disulfide-rich peptide toxin superfamilies (n=101) in Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae have originated from the 'primordial knot' named 'Adi Shakti'.
source: We propose that all of the extant spider disulfide-rich peptide toxin superfamilies (n=101) in Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae, which include those that were previously reported (n=26), as well as the ones identified in the present study (n=75), have originated from this 'primordial knot', further undergoing lineage-specific gene duplication and diversification (Figures 2—4).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The origin and diversification of spider toxin superfamilies can be explained by a mechanism similar to the combinatorial peptide strategy seen in cone snails.
source: The origin and diversification of these superfamilies can be explained by a mechanism that is similar to the combinatorial peptide strategy, wherein certain venomous animals, such as cone snails, generate a remarkable diversity in their mature toxin peptides while preserving the signal and propeptide regions (Escoubas and Rash, 2004; Zhu et al., 2000; Olivera et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cone snail venom evolution, supported by citations.

claim: Rapid events of diversification, preceded by repeated rounds of gene duplication, form the basis of the combinatorial peptide library strategy (Sollod et al., 2005).
source: Rapid events of diversification, preceded by repeated rounds of gene duplication, form the basis of the combinatorial peptide library strategy (Sollod et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the combinatorial peptide strategy supported by a citation.

claim: Hyper-mutational events in venom toxins have been shown to be restricted to the mature peptide regions (Conticello et al., 2001).
source: These hyper-mutational events have been previously shown to be restricted to the mature peptide regions of toxins (Conticello et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by a citation.

claim: The signal and propeptide regions of venom toxins evolve under the strong influence of negative selection pressures (Duda and Palumbi, 1999).
source: In contrast, the signal and propeptide regions, which are vital for the precise secretion and folding of proteins, respectively, evolve under the strong influence of negative selection pressures (Duda and Palumbi, 1999) - a molecular evolutionary trend also reported in venom coding genes of snakes (Brust et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about molecular evolution supported by citations.

claim: Cone snail venom coding genes have a recent evolutionary origin (<35–50 MYA; Olivera, 1997; Duda and Kohn, 2005).
source: However, unlike the cone snail venom coding genes that have a recent evolutionary origin (<35–50 MYA; Olivera, 1997; Duda and Kohn, 2005), spider venom toxins have likely originated from an ancestral scaffold in Opisthothelae, the clade that encompasses Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae spiders (over 99% of all spider genera described to date), nearly 375 MYA (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Spider venom toxins have likely originated from an ancestral scaffold in Opisthothelae nearly 375 MYA (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
source: However, unlike the cone snail venom coding genes that have a recent evolutionary origin (<35–50 MYA; Olivera, 1997; Duda and Kohn, 2005), spider venom toxins have likely originated from an ancestral scaffold in Opisthothelae, the clade that encompasses Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae spiders (over 99% of all spider genera described to date), nearly 375 MYA (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on phylogenetic dating and supported by a citation.

claim: Opisthothelae encompasses over 99% of all spider genera described to date.
source: However, unlike the cone snail venom coding genes that have a recent evolutionary origin (<35–50 MYA; Olivera, 1997; Duda and Kohn, 2005), spider venom toxins have likely originated from an ancestral scaffold in Opisthothelae, the clade that encompasses Mygalomorphae and Araneomorphae spiders (over 99% of all spider genera described to date), nearly 375 MYA (Magalhaes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The majority of positively selected sites (~96%) in spider venom DRP toxins were restricted to the mature peptide region.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the majority of positively selected sites (~96%) identified in spider venom DRP toxins (all sites in Araneomorphae, and all but two sites in Mygalomorphae) were restricted to the mature peptide region, whereas the signal and propeptide regions harboured a minor proportion of these sites (1% and 3%, respectively; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular evolutionary analyses.

claim: It has been theorised that the plesiotypic (or ancestral) DRP scaffold comprised of eight cysteines that formed four disulfide bonds (Pineda et al., 2020; Cole and Brewer, 2021).
source: It has been theorised that the plesiotypic (or ancestral) DRP scaffold comprised of eight cysteines that formed four disulfide bonds (Pineda et al., 2020; Cole and Brewer, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about prior theoretical work supported by citations.

claim: DRP toxins in extant spiders are comprised of distinct scaffolds with a range of cysteine pairs (4–12 cysteines forming 2–6 disulfide bonds).
source: As a result, we find that DRP toxins in extant spiders are comprised of distinct scaffolds with a range of cysteine pairs (4–12 cysteines forming 2–6 disulfide bonds).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis of DRP toxins.

claim: Venomous snakes have 'recruited' a myriad of toxins, including snake venom metalloproteinases, snake venom serine proteases, three-finger toxins, phospholipase A2s, L-amino acid oxidases, Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors, kallikreins, lectins, DNases, and hyaluronidases (Casewell et al., 2013; Faisal et al., 2021; Dutta et al., 2017; Senji Laxme et al., 2019a; Casewell et al., 2020; Figure 6).
source: Venomous snakes, for example, have 'recruited' a myriad of toxins, including snake venom metalloproteinases, snake venom serine proteases, three-finger toxins, phospholipase A2s, L-amino acid oxidases, Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors, kallikreins, lectins, DNases, and hyaluronidases (Casewell et al., 2013; Faisal et al., 2021; Dutta et al., 2017; Senji Laxme et al., 2019a; Casewell et al., 2020; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about snake venoms supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Spider venoms typically possess many forms of enzymes (e.g. phospholipases, proteases and chitinases), polyamines, salts, and disulphide-rich toxins (King and Hardy, 2013; Figure 6).
source: Similarly, spider venoms typically possess many forms of enzymes (e.g. phospholipases, proteases and chitinases), polyamines, salts, and disulphide-rich toxins (King and Hardy, 2013; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a statement about spider venom composition supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Spider venom DRPs with diverse ion channel targeting activities, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride ion channels, predominate in the venoms of nearly all spiders, constituting three-quarters of the venom.
source: However, spider venom DRPs with diverse ion channel targeting activities, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride ion channels, predominate in the venoms of nearly all spiders, constituting three-quarters of the venom (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Instead of recruiting distinct toxins with diverse functions into their venoms like the majority of venomous animals, spiders have diversified a single molecular template to generate commensurate functional diversity in their venoms.
source: Thus, instead of recruiting distinct toxins with diverse functions into their venoms like the majority of venomous animals, spiders seem to have diversified a single molecular template to generate a commensurate functional diversity in their venoms.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on comparative analysis of venom evolution.

claim: Mygalomorph DRP toxin superfamilies formed lineage-specific toxin clades (63/66) that suggested the recruitment of unique DRP scaffolds at the level of Linnaean genera.
source: Mygalomorph DRP toxin superfamilies formed lineage-specific toxin clades (63/66) that suggested the recruitment of unique DRP scaffolds at the level of Linnaean genera (Figure 2), while the majority of unique DRP scaffolds seemed to be recruited ancestrally at the level of Linnaean families in Araneomorphae (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of unique DRP scaffolds in Araneomorphae seemed to be recruited ancestrally at the level of Linnaean families.
source: Mygalomorph DRP toxin superfamilies formed lineage-specific toxin clades (63/66) that suggested the recruitment of unique DRP scaffolds at the level of Linnaean genera (Figure 2), while the majority of unique DRP scaffolds seemed to be recruited ancestrally at the level of Linnaean families in Araneomorphae (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Only a minor fraction (6/38) of araneomorph toxin superfamilies were recruited at the level of Linnaean genera.
source: Only a minor fraction (6/38) of araneomorph toxin superfamilies were recruited at the level of Linnaean genera.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analyses.

claim: A strong influence of positive selection was identified on the evolution of mygalomorph toxin superfamilies, with the majority (12/19) experiencing diversifying selection (ω between 1.19 and 2.95; PS: 0–26).
source: When the nature and strength of selection on venom DRPs were assessed, a strong influence of positive selection was identified on the evolution of these toxin superfamilies in mygalomorph spiders. Only a minority of these toxin superfamilies were found to be evolving under negative selection (6/19), or under near neutral evolution (1/19), while the majority (12/19) experienced diversifying selection (ω between 1.19 and 2.95; PS: 0–26, Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular evolutionary analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: The evolution of venom superfamilies (21/22) in Araneomorphae was constrained by purifying selection (ω between 0.03 and 0.97; PS: 1–3).
source: In complete contrast, the evolution of venom superfamilies (21/22) in Araneomorphae was constrained by purifying selection (ω between 0.03 and 0.97; PS: 1–3, Figure 5), and a single superfamily was found to be evolving nearly neutrally (ω of 1.0; PS: 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular evolutionary analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: The majority of replacements in mygalomorph spiders (between 0 and 29 properties) had a radical effect on the structure and/or biochemical property of the encoded toxin.
source: Outcomes of these evaluations suggest that the majority of replacements in mygalomorph spiders (between 0 and 29 properties) had a radical effect on the structure and/or biochemical property of the encoded toxin, while none were identified in most toxin superfamilies of Araneomorphae.
evidence: This is a finding from TreeSAAP analyses assessing biochemical property changes.

claim: A greater prevalence of episodic diversifying selection was detected on mygalomorph DRP toxin superfamilies than their araneomorph counterparts (0–34 versus 0–6 events, respectively).
source: We detected a greater prevalence of episodic diversifying selection on mygalomorph DRP toxin superfamilies than their araneomorph counterparts (0–34 versus 0–6 events, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from MEME analyses detecting episodic selection.

claim: Spiders of the genera Hadronyche and Atrax (family Atracidae) are known to deploy their DRP toxin superfamily (SF13: Ares) predominantly for antipredatory defence (Herzig et al., 2020).
source: Spiders of the genera, Hadronyche and Atrax (family Atracidae), are known to deploy their DRP toxin superfamily (SF13: Ares) predominantly for antipredatory defence (Herzig et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about toxin function supported by a citation.

claim: Tarantulas of the family Theraphosidae are known to mostly employ their venom to capture prey animals.
source: In contrast, tarantulas of the family Theraphosidae are known to mostly employ their venom to capture prey animals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about theraphosid spider behavior.

claim: Theraphosid spider venom DRPs deployed for prey capture reveal a strong influence of diversifying selection (ω: 1.2–2.9; PS: 0–11).
source: Our analyses of the molecular evolutionary histories of theraphosid spider venom DRPs deployed for prey capture reveal a strong influence of diversifying selection (ω: 1.2–2.9; PS: 0–11; Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), whereas those employed for self-defence in Atracidae spiders were constrained by negative selection (ω: 0.8; PS: 3; Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparative molecular evolutionary analyses.

claim: Defensive toxins employed for self-defence in Atracidae spiders were constrained by negative selection (ω: 0.8; PS: 3).
source: Our analyses of the molecular evolutionary histories of theraphosid spider venom DRPs deployed for prey capture reveal a strong influence of diversifying selection (ω: 1.2–2.9; PS: 0–11; Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), whereas those employed for self-defence in Atracidae spiders were constrained by negative selection (ω: 0.8; PS: 3; Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparative molecular evolutionary analyses.

claim: FUBAR identified numerous sites (~10%) in defensive toxins as evolving under the pervasive influence of negative selection.
source: Outcomes of FUBAR and MEME analyses further corroborated these findings. FUBAR identified numerous sites (~10%) in defensive toxins as evolving under the pervasive influence of negative selection, while MEME detected several episodically diversifying sites (~22%) in theraphosid toxins deployed for prey capture (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from FUBAR analyses shown in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: MEME detected several episodically diversifying sites (~22%) in theraphosid toxins deployed for prey capture.
source: Outcomes of FUBAR and MEME analyses further corroborated these findings. FUBAR identified numerous sites (~10%) in defensive toxins as evolving under the pervasive influence of negative selection, while MEME detected several episodically diversifying sites (~22%) in theraphosid toxins deployed for prey capture (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from MEME analyses shown in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Venom proteins are theorised to follow a 'two-speed' mode of evolution, wherein they readily diversify in animals that experience drastic shifts in ecology and/or environment.
source: Venom proteins are theorised to follow a 'two-speed' mode of evolution, wherein they readily diversify in animals that experience drastic shifts in ecology and/or environment - a prominent feature of evolutionarily younger lineages [e.g. cone snails and advanced snakes with evolutionary origins dating back to <35–50 MYA (Sunagar and Moran, 2015)].
